name: George Harrison
milestone_by_age_26: As lead guitarist of The Beatles, Harrison achieved a UK number-one single with 'Please Please Me' in early 1963 (age 20) and international fame with the band's Ed Sullivan Show appearance in February 1964 (age 21); by age 26 the Beatles were the biggest band in the world.
early_history_summary: Harrison grew up in a working-class family in Liverpool, became fascinated by rock and roll after hearing Elvis Presley's 'Heartbreak Hotel' at age 13, and got his first guitar at 14. He joined the Quarrymen (John Lennon's skiffle group) at 15 in 1958, which evolved into The Beatles. The band honed their craft through extended residencies in Hamburg clubs (1960-62) before signing with EMI and releasing their first hit single in 1962-63.
family_context_summary: Born to Harold Hargreaves Harrison, a bus conductor and former ship's steward, and Louise French, a shop assistant of Irish Catholic descent, in a working-class Liverpool household. His mother was particularly supportive of his musical interests, buying him his first guitar for £3.10s. The family lived in a council house in Speke.
parent_family_domain_summary: No direct music industry connections in the family; father was a bus conductor. However, his mother was an enthusiastic music fan with a loud singing voice, and she actively supported George's musical interests from a young age.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Beatles collaboration, Liverpool scene, Hamburg residencies, British Invasion, mother's support
evidence_summary: George Harrison joined the Quarrymen at 15 (1958), which became The Beatles, and achieved a UK number-one single by age 20 (1963) and global fame by 21 (1964 Ed Sullivan Show). His working-class Liverpool upbringing offered no financial advantages, but the city's port-city access to American records and the Merseybeat scene provided a frontier geography. The Lennon-McCartney-Harrison collaboration was an exceptionally high-trust peer team, and the British Invasion was a massive structural wave. His mother's support (buying his first guitar) was a meaningful family-domain advantage, though the family had no music industry connections.

name: Niki Lauda
milestone_by_age_26: Won his first Formula One World Drivers' Championship in 1975 (age 26) with Ferrari, having taken his maiden F1 victory at the 1974 Spanish Grand Prix (age 25) and won the British Formula Two Championship in 1972 (age 23).
early_history_summary: Born into a wealthy Vienna family (grandson of industrialist Hans Lauda), Lauda defied his family's disapproval to pursue racing, starting in karting and Formula Vee in the late 1960s. He took out a £30,000 bank loan secured by a life insurance policy to buy his way into Formula Two with March Engineering in 1971, making his F1 debut that year. He won the British F2 Championship in 1972, moved to BRM in 1973, and joined Ferrari in 1974, where he won his first Grand Prix and became World Champion in 1975.
family_context_summary: Born to a wealthy paper manufacturing family in Vienna; his paternal grandfather was industrialist Hans Lauda. His family strongly disapproved of his racing ambitions, leading to a feud and estrangement. He financed his early career with bank loans rather than family money.
parent_family_domain_summary: Family wealth came from paper manufacturing (grandfather Hans Lauda was a Viennese industrialist), but the family had no motorsport connections and actively opposed Lauda's racing career, providing no domain advantage.
primary_early_advantage_tags: wealthy family, bank loan, Formula Vee, Ferrari, family disapproval, early racing
evidence_summary: Niki Lauda won his first F1 World Championship at 26 (1975), capping a rapid rise from Formula Vee in the late 1960s to F1 debut in 1971 to Ferrari victory in 1974. Despite being born into a wealthy industrialist family (grandfather Hans Lauda), his family opposed racing and he financed his career through bank loans, creating a constraint-driven path. His natural driving talent and intense concentration were evident from his F2 success (British F2 Champion 1972) and rapid ascent through F1 teams. The F1 ecosystem provided an elite performance pipeline, and his move to Ferrari in 1974 was the key network breakthrough.

name: David Bowie

He studied art, music, and design, received saxophone lessons from Ronnie Ross, and trained in dramatic arts under Lindsay Kemp. After several failed singles and a flop debut album (1967), 'Space Oddity' became his first hit in 1969, timed with the Apollo 11 moon landing.

parent_family_domain_summary: No direct music industry connections in the family. His half-brother Terry Burns introduced him to modern jazz (Charles Mingus, John Coltrane), which influenced his early musical direction. His mother supported his musical interests by purchasing his first saxophone.

evidence_summary: David Bowie achieved his first UK chart hit with 'Space Oddity' at age 22 (1969, UK #5) and his major breakthrough with Ziggy Stardust at 25 (1972). He received saxophone lessons from Ronnie Ross and studied dramatic arts under Lindsay Kemp, building a unique combination of musical and theatrical skills. His working-class background offered no financial safety, but the cultural richness of 1960s London and his half-brother's jazz influence shaped his artistic direction.

name: Muhammad Yunus
milestone_by_age_26: Received a Fulbright scholarship in 1965 (age 25) to study economics at Vanderbilt University in the United States, after having become a lecturer in economics at Chittagong College in 1961 (age 21) and completing BA and MA degrees at Dhaka University by 1961.
early_history_summary: Born in Hathazari, Chittagong, to a Bengali Muslim family, Yunus excelled academically (ranking 16th out of 39,000 students in East Pakistan matriculation exams) and earned BA (1960) and MA (1961) degrees in economics from Dhaka University. He became a lecturer at Chittagong College at 21, set up a profitable packaging factory on the side, and then received a Fulbright scholarship in 1965 to pursue a PhD at Vanderbilt University, completing it in 1969.
family_context_summary: Born to Haji Muhammad Dula Mia Saudagar, a Sufi jeweller, and Sufia Khatun, as the third of nine children in a Bengali Muslim family in the village of Bathua, Chittagong District. The family moved to Chittagong city in 1944. His mother suffered psychological illness by 1949.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a jeweller (Saudagar); no direct economics or academic background in the family. However, the family valued education, and Yunus's academic excellence was evident from his high matriculation ranking.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Dhaka University, Fulbright scholarship, high academic ability, development economics, Vanderbilt
evidence_summary: Muhammad Yunus received a Fulbright scholarship at 25 (1965) to study at Vanderbilt University, a material and independently verifiable milestone, after becoming an economics lecturer at Chittagong College at 21. His academic excellence (16th out of 39,000 in matriculation) earned him entry to Dhaka University and then the Fulbright pipeline. His father was a jeweller in Chittagong, providing a modest middle-class background but no academic domain advantage. Mentors Nurul Islam and Rehman Sobhan at Dhaka University guided his early research. His later Nobel Prize (2006) came from pioneering microcredit, but the Fulbright scholarship and lectureship were material milestones by age 26.

name: Jochen Rindt
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 24 Hours of Le Mans in 1965 (age 23) paired with Masten Gregory in a Ferrari 250LM, and was an established Formula One driver with Cooper by age 26, having made his F1 debut in 1964 (age 22) and secured a full-time F1 drive for 1965.
early_history_summary: Born in Mainz, Germany, and orphaned at 15 months when his parents were killed in a WWII bombing raid, Rindt was raised by maternal grandparents in Graz, Austria. He started racing at 19 (1961) in his grandmother's Simca, progressed through Formula Junior and Formula Two, and made his F1 debut in 1964. He won the 24 Hours of Le Mans in 1965 at age 23 and signed a three-year F1 contract with Cooper. By 1968 he had moved to Brabham and then to Lotus in 1969, where he won his first F1 race and the 1970 World Championship (posthumously).
family_context_summary: Born to an Austrian mother and German father in Mainz, Germany. Parents owned a spice mill, which Rindt later inherited. Both parents were killed in a WWII bombing raid when he was 15 months old; he was raised by maternal grandparents in Graz, Austria. His mother had been a successful tennis player and studied law, as did his grandfather.
parent_family_domain_summary: No motorsport connections in the family. Parents owned a spice mill (inherited by Rindt), providing some financial means. Mother was a successful tennis player, suggesting athletic genes, but no direct racing domain transfer.

evidence_summary: Jochen Rindt won the 24 Hours of Le Mans at 23 (1965) and was an established F1 driver by 26, marking clear material milestones. The inherited spice mill provided modest financial means, and the Austrian/Central European racing scene gave him proximity to the sport. His Le Mans victory in 1965 was a landmark endurance racing achievement at a young age.
